title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1,000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2,000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream deterministic validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (> 0.05) and therefore the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis is not supported. A preregistered descriptive paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]; we report that bootstrap CI as a descriptive summary and explicitly label any one‑sided McNemar computations as exploratory/post‑hoc because a one‑sided test was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared initial = 1,000; repair = 5). We present the exact preregistered confirmatory result as the primary scientific outcome and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in the context of near‑unity baseline validity, sparse discordant counts, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations offers potential efficiency gains but poses safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command lists into harmful operational changes. Recent surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that degrade correctness for code and configuration generation, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates downstream deterministic validation and at‑most‑one repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our research question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the identical sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate), to what degree can a downstream deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes relative to reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally holds first‑pass generation constant so any paired difference is attributable only to deterministic validation and permitted repair.
sections.related_work:
Work on LLMs for structured outputs repeatedly documents hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and generation errors that reduce correctness for code and configuration tasks [1],[2]. Constrained decoding and schema‑aware planning have been shown to reduce syntactic and executable errors in several structured domains, though many demonstrations originate outside NetOps and therefore depend on validator/tool fidelity when applied to networking [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers present prototypes and evaluations of verifier‑assisted repair, guarded architectures, and governance/proof‑carrying proposals; these works emphasize that operational reliability depends on validator coverage, protocol enforcement, and external governance rather than on any single model alone [4],[5],[6].

Our study complements these works by preregistering a paired estimand that isolates the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation and a single limited repair call when the initial candidate is held constant across conditions. This isolates downstream mechanisms from first‑pass prompt/decoding or sampling variability and clarifies what a validator+repair layer can accomplish under tightly controlled conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen design. The study preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was finalized and frozen prior to any hosted‑model invocation; its SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest (ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec). Key preregistered elements: confirmatory paired binary design; task_count = 1,000 deterministic tasks drawn from a synthetic challenging workflow stress corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries included a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) and preregistered sensitivity analyses for failure handling.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and interpretation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the baseline and guarded episodes start from the same sampled candidate; the guarded pipeline may deterministically reject that candidate and may invoke at most one permitted repair call. Therefore, under our design any paired outcome differences arise only from deterministic validator decisions and permitted repair(s). The study does not measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generation arms, prompt re‑engineering, or constrained decoding because those arms were not executed under the preregistration.

Model and runtime configuration. The declared provider/model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The orchestration adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the deterministic validator/digital‑twin used was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The validator enforces workflow policies, required sequence presence and ordering, protected‑field noninterference, and returns a deterministic binary safe‑deploy verdict per task manifest.

Task corpus, selection, and validation. Tasks were selected deterministically from the preregistered corpus using the frozen selection rule to produce exactly 1,000 unique tasks. Each task manifest encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty labels. The deterministic validator compares parsed candidate command sequences against these manifest constraints in a deterministic emulator and emits structured traces that were archived for analysis.

Execution accounting, retries, and missingness. The preregistration limited retries and prespecified missingness treatments. The execution manifest records that all planned paired episodes were completed and that the adapter performed a small number of permitted repair calls. The primary analysis used the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' treatment; preregistered sensitivity analyses were available if missingness or adapter failures had occurred.
sections.results:
Execution and primary paired outcomes. The run completed all preregistered pairs. The 2×2 paired contingency table is: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred; total model calls used = 1,005 (shared initial = 1,000; repair = 5).

Inferential hierarchy and prespecified confirmatory test. The preregistered confirmatory analysis is the exact two‑sided McNemar test applied to the paired contingency table. That preregistered confirmatory test returns p = 0.0625 (> 0.05); under our frozen analysis plan this means the preregistered H1 is not supported. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was a preregistered descriptive summary and equals [0.001, 0.01]. Because a one‑sided McNemar was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration, any one‑sided McNemar computations are reported explicitly as exploratory/post‑hoc and do not alter the preregistered confirmatory conclusion.

Why the bootstrap CI can exclude zero despite a nonsignificant two‑sided McNemar. With near‑unity baseline validity the number of discordant pairs is very small (n10 + n01 = 5). Bootstrap percentile intervals, computed by resampling paired outcomes, are sensitive to such sparse discordant counts and the chosen resampling seed; under these conditions percentiles can produce small nonzero bounds even when an exact two‑sided paired test does not pass α = 0.05. We therefore present the bootstrap interval as a descriptive diagnostic and retain the exact two‑sided McNemar as the preregistered confirmatory result.

Representative repair diagnostics. Representative archived validator traces show repair invocations for required_sequence violations or protected‑field touches; in each recorded repair the adapter invoked a single permitted repair call and the validator accepted the repaired candidate on revalidation. The small number of repair events constrains inference about repair effectiveness across diverse failure modes.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory outcome and interpretation. The preregistered confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) is the primary inferential outcome and it did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI and any one‑sided McNemar reported are descriptive or exploratory: they provide diagnostic context but do not overturn the preregistered confirmatory null because the one‑sided test was not prespecified.

Mechanistic implications within shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because both conditions reused the identical sampled initial candidate, observed paired improvements can only stem from deterministic validator acceptance/rejection decisions and the single permitted repair. The five observed repairs demonstrate that a deterministic validator with appropriate rules can correct some ordering/sequence violations, but the small repair count could reflect low initial violation prevalence in the synthetic corpus, model+prompt behavior producing largely valid initial candidates, or validator coverage that omits other semantic error classes. Distinguishing among these requires preregistered follow‑ups that vary generator semantics, repair budget, and validator rule collections.

Threats to validity and external generalizability. Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the deterministic validator's rule coverage; omitted policy checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics deliberately isolates downstream effects but preclude measuring first‑pass prompt/decoding interventions. External validity: evaluation used a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a synthetic corpus validated by a deterministic digital twin; results do not automatically generalize to heterogeneous vendor equipment, other model families, or open production topologies. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power plan assumed a much lower baseline success rate (≈0.60) and a larger target effect (0.15); the observed baseline near 0.995 yields very few discordant pairs and limits statistical sensitivity for small absolute improvements.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment with shared_initial_candidate semantics (1,000 pairs), a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) versus a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625) and thus the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis is not supported. Only five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls used = 1,005. These artifact‑grounded results show that downstream deterministic validation and bounded repair can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflow scenarios, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and repair budget. Preregistered follow‑ups should (a) evaluate independent first‑pass generation arms to measure prompt/decoding interventions, (b) sweep repair budgets to quantify marginal returns per failure class, (c) expand validator rules and topology heterogeneity to probe external validity, and (d) include multiple model families to map model dependence. All follow‑ups should be preregistered with power calculations aligned to plausible baseline failure rates.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
